1:
The first proverb sets a dry crust against a full house, and they differ over what fills it. Keil and Delitzsch deny that the word means sacrificial gifts and insist it always means slain animals; it is the old name for the peace offerings, part of which went on the altar while part was served as a feast, so that what is described is a festival kept in hatred. Ellicott takes the same view and adds that the consuming of such offerings degenerated at times into licence. Gill works on the other half, taking the dry morsel for bread with nothing to eat alongside it.

Henry draws the moral. There may be peace where there are not three meals a day, he says, provided there is a joint satisfaction in the providence of God and a mutual satisfaction in each other prudence; holy love may be found in a cottage. His summary is that love will sweeten a dry morsel while strife will sour a house full of sacrifices. Clarke says the same more briefly, that domestic peace is beyond all other blessings.

The wise servant who rules a shameful son is illustrated rather than analysed. Henry states the principle twice, that true merit does not go by dignity, and that true dignity does go by merit, so that a prudent servant may gain such an interest with his master as to be taken in for a child share of the estate. Ellicott adds a case, of a servant who by timely help to a king obtained the property of his master, and observes that slaves born in the house often rose to positions of great trust, one steward having been heir presumptive until a son was born. Gill notes only that a servant who behaves well is set over the wayward son as a tutor.

On the fining pot they converge on affliction. Keil and Delitzsch call it an emblematical proverb, God being to the heart what the smelting pot is to silver, a trier of its nature and contents. Henry adds that the pot both proves and improves the metal, so that God searches whether hearts are standard and refines those that are; and he marks the limit of the comparison, that men may try their silver with a fining pot but have no way of trying one another hearts. Clarke describes the affliction as penetrating the soul and giving a man to see his own state, and Ellicott as sorrows allowed to assail men so that they may come out of the trial as pure gold.

On the man who listens to false lips Keil and Delitzsch make a grammatical point that changes the force of the verse: the clause does not describe what a profligate does but stamps as a profligate whoever does it. Henry takes both halves as a circle, that those who design ill support themselves with falsehood, and that a liar listens to a backbiting tongue in order to have something on which to graft his own lies; those who court the acquaintance of the bad show what they are. Wesley reads the false lips as accusations that give a man occasion to do mischief, and Clarke that an evil heart is ever ready to receive evil.

Keil and Delitzsch give the last of the five its ground: the poor man, as a man and as poor, is the work of God, so that mocking him mocks the one who called him into existence and appointed him his lowly place. They add that gladness at calamity is a mortal sin even where the sufferer is an enemy. Henry says God can reduce us to that condition, and that whoever would be built up on the ruins of others shall have the same cup put into his own hand; Clarke, that a man pleased to hear of another misfortune will find his own multiplied.
6:
Keil and Delitzsch render the sixth verse as a diadem of the old being children of children. A family circle of children and grandchildren is a crown encircling the grey-haired man; and on the other side, to have a man of honoured name for a father is the most effective commendation a son can have. From the second clause they derive the fact of experience out of which inherited nobility has proceeded, since a man may abnegate his social rights and yet remain part of the moral order of the world. Gill adds that the honour is greatest when the children walk in the way they were trained.

Keil and Delitzsch observe that the next four proverbs appear joined acrostically, and then work on the key word of the seventh. They reject three renderings, elevated, diffuse and imperative, and settle on presumptuous, words of superfluity; such speech makes the impression of the speaker vulgarity the more repulsive. Ellicott agrees, preferring superfluous or pretentious words, and would render the second half liberal person rather than prince, summing it in the maxim that nobility obliges. Henry finds two absurdities here, that men of no repute should set up as dictators and that men of great repute should deceive; lying ill becomes any man, but worst of all a prince, and he quotes the saying that whoever knows not how to dissemble knows not how to reign. Clarke turns the proverb on public speakers who affect a fine language suiting neither their conversation nor their education, such words being as unbecoming as a cart wheel among clockwork.

The proverb about the gift raises a question of who is meant in the second clause. Keil and Delitzsch argue that the person and not the gift must be the subject, since the verb is used only of persons, and decide that the man in view is the one to whom the present is brought rather than the one who has it to give. Gill leaves both open, reporting one authority for the giver and another for the receiver, who will do anything the giver directs. Ellicott takes it as a description of the influence of bribery, and observes that the constant warnings against it from the earliest law down to the prophets show how prevalent it was. Henry gives the two sides their sharpest form, that those with money in their hand think they can do anything with it, the deepest bag carrying the cause, and that those with money in their eye will do anything for it. Wesley cautions that this proverb, like many others, holds of most men and not of all.

On covering a transgression Keil and Delitzsch supply the image the verse wants: a man proves love who does not strike the great bell when his neighbour has sinned against him; and seeking love here means not winning the love of another but preserving love among men. Henry puts the practice into three sentences, that an oversight should be overlooked, that what was done through forgetfulness should be forgotten, and that what made nothing of us should be made nothing of; the ripping up of faults, he says, is the ripping out of love, and the best method of peace is an act of oblivion.

On the last of the five Gill notes that the reproof descends, as the word signifies, into the heart of a wise man. Keil and Delitzsch call it one of the few proverbs beginning with a future; they canvass a variant found in two ancient versions and derived from another root, and ask whether the traditional text needs correcting at all. Henry sets the two halves as portraits, a word being enough for the wise while stripes are not enough for a fool, and instances a king softened by three words of rebuke against one who stayed hard under a succession of plagues.
11:
Keil and Delitzsch head this group as five proverbs about dangerous men, and open with a question of grammar. Which word is subject and which object in the eleventh verse? They decide for rebellion as the subject, an abstract standing for a concrete, on the ground that seeking after evil is a far more natural connection of ideas than seeking after rebellion; the sense is that the rebellious man seeks only evil. On the cruel messenger the readings run from the human to the angelic: Ellicott thinks of the chief of the executioners, always ready to carry out the bidding of an eastern king, Wesley of a cruel angel or of bloody men employed by God, and Henry of a dreadful judgment sent as a messenger.

On the bear Keil and Delitzsch notice that the noun keeps its masculine form even when the female is meant; the state of folly, they explain, is a paroxysm of anger, since folly morbidly heightened is madness. Henry turns it into two charges, that a passionate man is a brutish man, and that he is a dangerous man, falling foul of whoever stands in his way. Anger, he says, is a temporary madness, and one may more easily escape an enraged bear than an outrageous angry man.

The next proverb is graded rather than condemned. Keil and Delitzsch place ingratitude among the manifestations of ignoble selfishness and ask how much more sinful is the black ingratitude that recompenses evil for good. Henry states the same scale in a sentence, that to render evil for evil is brutish but to render evil for good is devilish; the curse is entailed on the family, the crime being heinous enough to be punished not in the person only but in the posterity.

The letting out of water is the best worked figure in the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch establish the verb as meaning to break forth, noting that one ancient version took it in the legal sense of setting free but that here it means the man who tears the dam away from the waters. Their rendering of the second half is to cease from such strife before it comes to the showing of teeth, and Ellicott gives the same phrase the same sense, a metaphor taken from an angry dog. Ellicott also supplies the picture, that the drops oozing through a tiny hole in the bank of a reservoir soon swell into an unmanageable torrent. Clarke describes the same failure mechanically, the water pressing from all parts toward the smallest breach until dike and all are swept away. Henry draws the practical rule twice: dread the breaking of the ice, for once broken it will break further, and leave the quarrel off not when you see the worst of it, when it may be too late, but when you see the first of it. Gill notes that the Hebrew order gives the man who lets out water as himself the beginning of strife, which some have understood of letting water into a neighbour field and so occasioning lawsuits.

On the last of the five Keil and Delitzsch aim the proverb at the partisan judge open to bribery; and although the man who acquits the guilty appears as if he must be judged more mildly than the man who condemns the innocent, the proverb makes both alike an abhorrence to God. Henry presses that equality where it is hardest, that it is as provoking to justify the wicked, even in pity and to save a life, as to condemn the just, and extends the verse beyond the courts to private persons who plead for sin, and so confound the eternal distinction between good and evil. Ellicott notes that the perversion of justice was a fruitful source of evil and a constant topic of reproach in the mouth of the prophets.
16:
Keil and Delitzsch read the sixteenth verse as a single question rather than two, why the ready money in the hand of the fool to get wisdom when he has no heart to it, and dispute the accenting, holding the manuscripts right against most editions. Henry finds two things to wonder at: the goodness that puts a price into a foolish man hand, a talent held in possession and not out of reach, and the wickedness that has no skill nor will nor courage to improve it, having set its heart elsewhere. Gill takes the price for worldly substance, with which a man might buy useful books and procure himself instructors, but which he spends instead on his back and belly. Wesley glosses it as opportunities and abilities, wanting discretion to discern the worth of wisdom, and Ellicott adds that a man may pay high for instruction and remain a fool if he has no capacity for taking it in.

On the friend who loves at all times Keil and Delitzsch say the halves rise by degrees, brother being more than friend; the article marks out not any friend but the friend who answers to the idea of one, of whom alone it is said that he makes his love manifest. Henry distinguishes constancy from humour, since the fanciful and selfish love no longer than their interest is served and their affections turn with the wind; swallow-friends fly to you in summer and are gone in winter, and of such there is no loss. Gill calls a constant lover a very rare thing, and Clarke takes the second half of the ties of kindred, a brother born to support and comfort a brother in distress.

Suretyship follows at once, and Henry reads the sequence as a caution, that none under pretence of generosity to a friend should be unjust to his own family. To pass a word for an absent friend may be occasion enough, but to become surety in his very presence supposes his own word will not be taken, and then who can safely pass a word for him? Gill agrees that friendship does not oblige a man to risk the ruin of his household. Keil and Delitzsch argue against the common rendering for his neighbour, since that preposition never means on behalf of; the neighbour is rather the person with whom the bail is entered into.

The quarrelsome man and the man who exalts his gate are paired, and Keil and Delitzsch call quarrelsomeness and ostentation two symptoms of one selfishness, each bearing its sentence in itself: the first commits himself to the way of great sinning and draws others after him, while the second, unable to have his door high or splendid enough, prepares against his own will the destruction of his house. They quote an old saying that whoever busies himself with building grows poor. Clarke reports that doors in that country are kept low, not three feet, to keep horsemen from riding into the courts and spoiling the goods; but he thinks the gate may equally stand for the mouth and its exalting for arrogant speech that kindles strife, which he judges suits the context better. Henry says such a man makes his gate so large that his house and estate go out at it.

The froward heart closes the group. Ellicott grounds its want of good in the abomination such a heart is to God, and so it gains no blessing. Keil and Delitzsch render the parallel of one who twists with his tongue, going about concealing and falsifying the truth. Henry separates the halves as framing ill designs and giving ill language, the first unable to buy back the repose and reputation it costs, the second losing friends and provoking enemies; many have paid dearly for an unbridled tongue. Wesley says only that he shall not get the advantage he expects.
21:
Keil and Delitzsch mark this verse as opening a new part of the book, striking again the keynote of the fool with which an earlier division began and closed; they weigh whether the clause reads as a purpose or merely as a consequence. Gill notes that this means not an idiot but a wicked son who departs from his education and despises all parental counsel. Henry uses it to show how uncertain our creature-comforts are, the very thing in which we promised ourselves most satisfaction proving the greatest cross; there was joy when a man child was born, yet if he prove vicious his father will wish he had never been born. He adds that the afflicted parent must still make the best of it, since the fool is of his own begetting.

On the merry heart Keil and Delitzsch render it that a joyful heart brings good recovery, and set out the physiology: the heart is the centre of the individual life, while the spirit is the power of self-consciousness which, as it is lifted up or broken, lifts up or breaks down the body. They reject the ancient versions that render the rare word body, since another word is used for that. Clarke reports the same variant, that some copies read body rather than medicine, which makes the two halves answer each other exactly, and adds that nothing so directly ruins health as grief and anxiety. Gill offers three renderings, that a merry heart makes a good medicine, that it makes a medicine operate kindly, and that it makes the countenance serene. Henry warns that this is not a heart addicted to carnal mirth, which is madness and not medicine, and that mirth as a medicine must be taken sparingly and by rule. Wesley says plainly that cheerfulness contributes to bodily health and vigour.

Bribery from the bosom follows. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the word and the clause of purpose require a man in high judicial office; the gift is brought out from the fold of the clothing where it lay concealed and given into the bosom of him whose favour is bought, under four eyes and withdrawn from any third person. Clarke says he has often observed the purse carried in the bosom above the girdle. Ellicott gives the same picture of the folds of the dress in which the bribe was hidden, ready for the hand of the judge. Henry insists the giver is as bad as the taker, and that the man is ashamed even as he does it, concealing it so slyly that he would hide it from his own conscience; its power is such that the course of justice is not merely obstructed but turned into injustice, and the greatest wrongs done under colour of doing right.

The last of the four sets attention against distraction. Keil and Delitzsch report the common reading, that the understanding finds wisdom everywhere while the fool seeks it at the end of the world, but prefer another sense from the order of the words: wisdom lies before the eyes of the understanding as his aim, whereas the eyes of the fool, keeping nothing in view, roam about. Ellicott puts it simply, that she lies straight before him while the fool looks everywhere. Henry turns it on readiness, that an intelligent man has wisdom ready when he has occasion for it, laying it before him as his card and compass, whereas the man with a roving rambling fancy is fit for no solid business, his mind filled with a thousand impertinent things when it should be applied to his study. Gill takes the alternative rendering that wisdom is in the face of the understanding man, seen in a grave and composed countenance. Clarke adds that wisdom is within sight and reach of every man, but not likely to be found by one whose desires are scattered abroad.
25:
Keil and Delitzsch note that this series begins and closes as the one before it did, and that the verse links back to the earlier proverb on the father of a fool; they render it a grief to his father is a foolish son, and a bitter woe for her that bare him,. Henry divides the pain between the parents: the word used of the father signifies anger, since such children contemn it, while the mother has sorrow and bitterness because they abuse her tenderness. Being joint-sufferers, he says, they should comfort each other, the mother mollifying the father anger and the father alleviating the mother grief. Gill puts it down to the folly of the son and the ruin he is bringing on himself.

The next proverb Keil and Delitzsch treat as standing by itself, and they work at the opening particle. They ask whether it points back to a context from which the verse has been separated, or hints at many kinds of worthless men, or means that a fine on the righteous is also not good, and reject all three: the proverb must have a meaning complete in itself. Ellicott takes the punishing as fining especially, the striking as scourging, and the last phrase as meaning when they have acted uprightly. Henry sets the halves as duties on either side of a quarrel between rulers and subjects: rulers must never be a terror to good works, since when princes turn persecutors their thrones will be neither easy nor firm; and subjects must not find fault with the government for doing its duty. Wesley extends the striking to smiting with the tongue as well as the hand, and Clarke presses it hardest, that to take off the head of a ruler under pretence of his not being equitable is a dreadful omen to any land, no such experiment having ever promoted the public prosperity.

On sparing words Keil and Delitzsch render the first line that he who keeps his words to himself has knowledge, and the second that the cool of temper is a man of understanding. They canvass the written and marginal readings of the second phrase; one authority glosses it as a spirit held back and most take the spirit as expressing itself in words, but their own preference is for a weighty spirit, a quiet seriousness proceeding from high conscientiousness and maintaining itself in self-control. Ellicott renders it the same way. Gill reads the sparing two ways, as a fund of knowledge that thinks much and says little, and as a bridle that keeps a man from speaking hastily when provoked. Henry finds two marks of wisdom here, a sweet and sedate temper, since a cool head with a warm heart is an admirable composition, and a good government of the tongue, since words are better spared than ill spent.

The chapter closes on the value of silence. Keil and Delitzsch observe that the subject and predicate of the first line serve the second also, and that the verb for shutting, ordinarily used of the ear, is here transferred to the mouth; they gather an old proverb that silence is the covering of the stupid, and a line of verse to the effect that every uninstructed man is most prudent while he is silent. Gill says the fool will be reckoned wise by those who do not know him, since he does not betray his folly by his words, and in this one thing acts the wise part. Clarke agrees that he is wise as to that particular, a wise fool who knows he cannot speak well and has sense enough not to; a man may be golden-mouthed and silver-tongued in eloquence, but to know when and where to speak and to be silent is better than diamonds. Yet he ends on the difficulty, that whoever thinks he can speak well can hardly refrain.
